title: Ramakrishna and tantra's reputation
hook: a saint walks the whole tantric path, and the wine never reaches his lips
carry: the offering makes the rite, not the substance
tomorrow: who decides the order of a temple's whole day?

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bhringi tried to split them, and Shiva became half the goddess: Shiva and Shakti are never apart. Today, tantra's reputation, met head on.

Calcutta, the eighteen-sixties. In the temple garden at Dakshineswar lives a priest of the goddess Kali named Ramakrishna. One day a wandering woman teacher arrives, known as the Bhairavi Brahmani, deeply learned in the Tantras. For about two years, by his disciples' accounts, she leads him through one tantric discipline after another. Some of those rites use things the usual rules of worship keep out, wine among them. So what happens when the cup comes to the priest?
screen: `DAKSHINESWAR, THE 1860s.` → `A WOMAN TEACHER OF THE TANTRAS.` → `THEN THE CUP.`

segments.voice: The accounts say he couldn't drink it. He touched a drop to his forehead, already lost in the Mother, and that was all. Through every rite he saw each woman as the Mother herself. That's the true shape of tantra's reputation. Some rites, in some lineages, really did offer things the ordinary purity rules forbid, wine and meat among them. The idea was bold: if everything is the goddess's power, nothing is outside her, not even what the usual rules call unclean. But the Tantras guard their own door. The Kularnava Tantra says, in effect: if drinking wine brought perfection, every drunkard would be perfect; if eating meat did, every meat-eater would be holy. Done for appetite, the rite is no path at all. Here's the teaching. In tantra the substance isn't the rite. The offering is: knowing who it's for. Lineages answer this differently, and none is ranked here. Some call themselves the right-hand way, dakshina, and keep worship inside the familiar rules. Others follow the left-hand way, vama, where such rites belong, under a teacher and strict conditions. Many use substitutes, milk or fruit. So the rumor holds one true thread, cut loose from everything that held it in place.
screen: `HE TOUCHED IT TO HIS FOREHEAD.` · `NOTHING IS OUTSIDE HER.` · `APPETITE IS NO PATH.` · `RIGHT-HAND, LEFT-HAND, SUBSTITUTES.` · then, large: `THE OFFERING MAKES THE RITE.`

segments.voice: Many Hindus offer food and water to the deity before taking any themselves; what comes back is prasad, blessed. If there's water near you and you pray, offer it first in your mind, then take one sip and hold it: its coolness, its weight, the moment it goes down. If you don't, simply take the sip with your whole attention, and stay with the aftertaste for the rest of the sit.
What tantra actually is: here, a path whose own book says the substance isn't the rite, and appetite isn't a path.
Something to keep: the offering makes the rite, not the substance. Ramakrishna's cup showed it. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Tantric lineages differ: some keep to conventional worship, some perform rites with normally forbidden substances under a teacher, and some use substitutes or read them symbolically.

Kularnava.meaning: a Tantra that warns against rites done for appetite

dakshina.meaning: the right-hand way: worship within familiar rules

vama.meaning: the left-hand way, under a teacher and strict conditions

Ramakrishna.meaning: a 19th-century saint and priest of Kali at Dakshineswar

Bhairavi Brahmani.meaning: the woman teacher who guided Ramakrishna's tantric practice

prasad.meaning: food or water offered to the deity, then received back as blessed

sources.ref: Swami Saradananda, Sri Ramakrishna the Great Master (Ramakrishna's tantric disciplines under the Bhairavi Brahmani at Dakshineswar, early 1860s; his inability to take wine, touching it only to his forehead; his regard for every woman as the Mother)
Kularnava Tantra, chapter 2 (if perfection came merely from drinking wine, all drunkards would attain it; likewise meat)
Tantric tradition on dakshina (right-hand) and vama (left-hand) practice, and on symbolic readings and substitutes
